Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen Media San Francisco San Francisco-area estate sells for $70m in sign of AI-fueled wealth explosion New owner is said to be involved in AI industry, as new class of multimillionaires is entering the real estate race Sophie Sullivan Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.22 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A luxury Lake Como-inspired estate in the San Francisco Bay Area has sold to a buyer “in the AI world” for a record $70m, in the latest sign of a new tech wealth boom that’s pushing home prices to extraordinary heights in the region The property south of San Francisco not only becomes the most expensive sale in its affluent town of Hillsborough, doubling a previous record, but is also the most expensive sale in northern California this year, according to listing agent Jennifer Gilson of Golden Gate Sotheby’s International Realty. Gilson declined to share any details about the buyer, other than that the new owner of 3000 Ralston Avenue is a man in the AI industry. It is the latest sign of a housing boom across Silicon Valley being driven by AI wealth. Last month, an analysis found that more than 140 San Francisco homes have sold at least $1m above their asking price in the first six months of this year. View image in fullscreen The exterior of the property. Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen Media The property, known as “ Villa de Verano ”, was initially listed at $88m, and sat on the market for only four months and 22 days. Besides a six-bed, 12,400 sq ft home that is complete with its own gym, theater, spa and aquarium, the 12-acre property also features a pool, a rose garden, an amphitheater, a guest property and a sporting area fitted with seven courts and a putting green. Its opulence stands out even among other palatial Hillsborough homes, which include Bing Crosby’s $25m home, Elon Musk’s $32m former home and the Levi Strauss-connected $17.8m Koshland Estate. Yet Gilson says this sale is only a “stepping stone” into a market of homes catering to the incredibly wealthy. “Even in the last year, there’s been a major increase of buyers from the AI world,” she said. “This could be just the beginning of the ultra luxury.” View image in fullscreen The property’s pool and outdoor area. Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen Media Since the San Francisco-based companies OpenAI and Anthropic filed for initial public offerings earlier this summer, a new class of multimillionaires has entered the real estate race. An analysis by brokerage Compass described a “housing market increasingly segmented by income tier and proximity to AI-driven employment centers”. Gilson said she has seen an influx of wealth among buyers coming not just from AI companies, but increasingly from other, traditional industries. She described a “definite increase” in those ultra-rich buyers taking off-market, “hidden” opportunities, meaning Gilson connects buyers to sellers without homes ever being listed. In San Mateo county, where the sale took place, the median price of a single-family home increased by 8.5% between May 2025 and May 2026. San Francisco county saw a more than one-fifth increase, with median prices jumping from $1.8m to $2.2m. https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/worl.text: Tons of dead fish have been removed from the Gliwice Canal in southern Poland after a toxic golden algae bloom triggered a new environmental crisis in the Oder River system. Polish authorities said the fish deaths were linked to Prymnesium parvum, a microscopic organism capable of producing toxins that can be lethal to aquatic life. The incident has revived memories of the devastating 2022 Oder River ecological disaster, when hundreds of tonnes of fish and other wildlife died across the waterway. Authorities are now closely monitoring the affected canal and surrounding waters to prevent the outbreak from spreading further. The latest event also highlights the complex conditions that can allow golden algae to flourish, including elevated salinity, nutrient pollution, unusually warm temperatures and low water levels. Research and conservation groups have warned that these pressures could make similar ecological crises more likely as climate change intensifies.Toxic golden algae is behind the mass fish deathsThe immediate concern in the Gliwice Canal is Prymnesium parvum, commonly known as golden algae. The single-celled microalgae is capable of producing prymnesins, toxins that can severely damage the gills of fish and other aquatic organisms. Once the toxins enter the animalsâ bodies, they can cause extensive internal damage and death. Unlike many algae associated with freshwater ecosystems, Prymnesium parvum is particularly associated with brackish and saline environments. Under favourable conditions, however, it can proliferate rapidly in freshwater systems. The organism was identified as the key driver of the catastrophic 2022 fish die-off in the Oder, making its detection in the river system particularly concerning. The latest deaths have occurred in part of the Gliwice Canal, which is connected to the wider Oder basin. Polish authorities have been carrying out regular patrols on both land and water while monitoring conditions and removing dead fish from affected areas.Why the Oder River system is vulnerable to another algae crisisThe current situation is particularly worrying because it follows the enormous ecological disaster that struck the Oder in 2022. During that event, hundreds of tonnes of dead fish, clams, crayfish and other wildlife were found along the river. Investigations eventually linked the mass mortality to a large-scale bloom of Prymnesium parvum. The algae did not emerge in isolation. Researchers have described the 2022 disaster as a compound environmental event involving several pressures at the same time. High levels of salt, nutrients, hot water temperatures, and low flow in the rivers provided suitable conditions for rapid proliferation of the algae. This is still relevant. High temperature could lead to proliferation of harmful algae, and low flows to high levels of salt and nutrients. Water pollution could also change the chemistry of the water bodies in such a way that species that are normally found in low amounts can now dominate.How golden algae can kill fish so quicklyIt is the capability of Prymnesium parvum to release potent toxins referred to as prymnesins that represents a threat from this organism. Based on the results obtained within the AEGIS research project, these toxins are able to destroy the gills of fish, which gives rise to penetration into the blood and poisoning of internal organs. In this way, a large-scale development of Prymnesium parvum can result in massive death among fish. Moreover, the corpses of fish are evidence of the critical state of ecology of the ecosystem. Hence, a sharp increase in dead fish can be considered an indicator of changing conditions in water. It can produce energy through photosynthesis but can also feed on other organisms. This flexibility may help it survive and expand when environmental conditions shift in its favour.A warning for Polandâs waterwaysThe latest fish deaths show that the environmental problems associated with the Oder have not simply disappeared since the 2022 disaster. Prymnesium has become established within the Oder system and high concentrations have continued to be reported since the original catastrophe. For authorities, the priority is to contain the affected area and prevent the algae and its effects from spreading further through connected waterways. Continued monitoring is essential because changes in water temperature, salinity, nutrient levels and river flow can influence how quickly a bloom develops. The renewed fish deaths also demonstrate how vulnerable freshwater ecosystems can become when several environmental pressures occur simultaneously. As warming temperatures, intensive water use and persistent pollution place additional stress on rivers, scientists warn that compound ecological events could become more frequent or severe.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
